utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. May I ask this day for the appearances. I see a new face on the bench for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's right. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom. My name is Caitlin Chittenden. I'll be questioning the first witness in court today on behalf of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So the first witness we have today is Witness 114, who will also be known as the pseudonym PW-047. And he'll be testifying with face distortion, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in. While the witness is being brought in, Madam Registrar could read into the record information related to two exhibits received yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Exhibits P365B and Exhibit P368B, tendered through Witness PW-048, are marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please wait a moment so the windows can be opened again. Good afternoon again, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. As you know, there are protective measures in place for you, and the Prosecution has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: We met on Tuesday. My name is Caitlin Chittenden, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could we have P405 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see something coming up on the screen in front of you now. Please, could you read it to yourself and confirm that your name is written next to "PW-047."

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this into evidence as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic on 24 January 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your testimony at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to listen to your Popovic testimony again before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, I have, a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to offer into evidence the witness's testimony in the Popovic case. It is P403, which should be admitted under seal. And we also have 404, which is the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, the first under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also like to offer into evidence the four exhibits admitted in conjunction with this witness's testimony in the Popovic case. The first exhibit I would like to offer is P399, under seal. This is the witness's statement to the OTP on 24 January 2007, and this statement was admitted in Popovic as the underlying Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: At this time, I would also like to offer into evidence the three intercepts identified by the witness in his Popovic testimony and which were admitted as exhibits through him in that case. For each intercept, there's a handwritten version from the note-book and a typewritten print-out version of the intercept. And if I may, I'll just read out the P numbers for the following three intercepts. The first one is P400A, which is the B/C/S note-book version and the corresponding English translation. Do you want me to read them out in a list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, the whole list, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And P400B, which is the print-out version. Then we have P401A, the note-book version; P401B, the print-out version; P402A, the note-book version; and finally, P402B, the print-out version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The exhibits will be received, the confidential ones under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you very much. Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's testimony in Popovic. Witness, after I read out the summary, I'll just have a few further questions for you. Your Honours, if we may move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: At the southern site, the witness worked 10-day shifts. He described the procedure he used to intercept, record, and transcribe radio communications. When transcribing an intercept, the witness would often consult his colleagues if something on the tape was unclear. Another person would then type out his handwritten transcription of the conversation, after which the typed version of the intercept would be encrypted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: ... would be encrypted and sent out. On a few occasions, the witness typed up his handwritten transcriptions himself, but he did not transmit reports. During his 2007 OTP interview, the witness reviewed photocopies of three handwritten intercepts. For the record, these are the intercepts we just tendered with the witness's statement as P400A, P401A, and P402A. The witness confirmed that he was the operator who intercepted, recorded, and transcribed those three intercepts. The witness also reviewed three typewritten print-outs of the intercepts. For the record, these are the intercepts we just tendered as Exhibits 400B, 401B, and 402B. The witness confirmed that those print-outs contained the same conversations as the three intercepts he previously confirmed taking by hand. The witness noted that in one of his intercepts, which is Exhibit P401A, taken at 949 hours on 20 July 1995, he wrote in the note-book that Cerovic, one of the speakers, was a colonel or lieutenant-colonel, but in the print-out version of this intercept Cerovic is identified as a colonel. The witness does not specifically recall whether he made that change in consultation with his colleagues or whether the typist made the change alone. The witness stated that while there are one or two other minor differences between the handwritten and the typed versions, none of those differences changes the meaning of the intercept. That concludes my summary. Your Honours, I now have a few questions to ask the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a booklet of three intercepts that we've compiled. For the record, these are P400A and B, P401A and B, and P402A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could I ask for the assistance of the Court Usher just to hand this book to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a moment to look through this booklet, and let me know whether you recognise your handwriting on the handwritten versions of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, were you the operator who recorded and transcribed these three intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you review these three intercepts before you testified in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you review them again before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you also recently reviewed the original note-books containing those three intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And do the copies of those three intercepts that you have in the booklet conform to the original note-books that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, about how long after you intercepted and recorded a conversation on the tape would you transcribe that conversation into the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: We would take down shorter intercepts immediately and copied them into note-books, unless there was another conversation on the same frequency. If they followed each other closely, we would record both. And once all activity ceased on that particular channel, we would then note down both conversations into our note-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Would you say that you recorded into the note-books the conversation within 24 hours, say?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them we even recorded in the note-books immediately. Let me clarify. If there was no further activity on that same frequency, we would take the tape, immediately listen to it, and note it down into the note-books.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So with respect to the three intercepts in the booklet in front of you that you intercepted on 17, 20, and 22 July, can you attest to the Trial Chamber that you transcribed these conversations into the note-books within 24 hours of recording them?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And were the original note-books that you inspected with me on Tuesday the same original note-books that you recorded these conversations in during July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also have the three original note-books available with me in the courtroom today, should Your Honours or the accused wish to inspect them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, can you please turn to tab 2 in the booklet in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit P401A, if we can also have that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, if you can turn to the handwritten version, or you can look on the screen in front of you, you will see underneath "Colonel Cerovic" is written "Lieutenant-Colonel "in brackets. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why you wrote this in brackets in this instance?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Because once listening to a tape, you write things down immediately, but sometimes frequency modulations can slightly vary and it can make you doubtful as to whether what was uttered was "lieutenant-colonel" or "colonel," since the words are rather similar. However, from our previous knowledge, we knew that this was Colonel Cerovic, but we always left room for uncertainty. We usually did not write things down unless we were certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: But, Witness, at the time that you were listening to the recording and transcribing it, did you -- does this mean that you didn't hear the rank of Cerovic clearly at the time you were transcribing?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: One could say so. We couldn't hear the whole of the conversation completely clearly. We listened to two interlocutors, and sometimes they overlapped. And on occasion, you cannot hear things the best way possible. They didn't necessarily communicate clearly. For example, in this conversation, you can hear one of the people saying, Hello, sir, and then it is immediately followed by something which resembled either, Colonel, or, Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: But, Witness, did you ever write something down of which you were uncertain without recording it in some way?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Well, we can't say that we weren't certain about this, but we did have a slight reservation. The audiotape has to be reflected as accurately as possible on paper, but still there is a small hedge that you have to allow for, because it is then forwarded to other instances and they can verify that. In this case, we did note down that it was Colonel Cerovic, but just in case we put another thing in brackets. However, we always wrote down only what we could hear, and the words on paper reflect what we could hear on the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And is this generally how you would denote something you were uncertain of, by using brackets?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean when you say "generally"?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If when you were listening to a recording of a conversation, if you weren't certain of what you heard, would you put brackets around what you think it was?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: If we couldn't hear them, we would place three dots, for the most part. If we were uncertain, then we inserted brackets.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And if you're uncertain of something, did you also consult your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes, I did. All of the work was done in a single room, where we worked jointly, more or less. We would work together while listening to the tapes and noting down. We also always required assistance from either our commander or another work-mate who happened to be there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please now turn over a couple of pages in that book, still behind tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: In e-court, it's P401B, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: You can also look at it on the screen. So this is the print-out version, 401B.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can also have that in e-court, please. Thank you. And it should have a corresponding English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, in your 2007 statement, you noted that in this printed version of the intercept which we're looking at now, Cerovic is identified as a colonel. But as we've just seen and talked about, in the handwritten version Cerovic is identified as either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel. Witness, do you have any explanation as to why there is this difference between the printed and the handwritten versions?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: When transcription is being done of an audio-recording, you write things down the way you hear them. However, in the next phase it had to be typed up and sent following encryption. The principal operator or the commander, whomever happened to be on duty that day, typed up the final report. Colonel Cerovic was someone we had known from before, so the commander or the operator inserted the word "Colonel." They were familiar with it, and they knew whether a person was a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, and this is why in this report it is stated that he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: But, Witness, did you engage in any analysis or interpretation of intercepts yourself?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: What do you mean, "analysis or interpretation"? We wrote them down, and then we would read it out loud to the commander or the operator while they were typing it up and encrypting it. We used Paket communication to send it on to our command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So, Witness, you wrote down only what you heard?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you know now Mr. Tolimir has the right to cross-examine you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace be with this house. I would like to greet the witness and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the statement please be shown on the screen. The number is P399. Could we please see page 2. I'm interested in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see what you stated in item 4? In item 4, you stated that with a group which is mentioned in here, from the beginning of 1995 to October 1995, you left the unit for health reasons, but you did not state whether before 1995 you worked with that group.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No, I didn't work with that group until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you also stated that you were sent to serve in the Unit for Anti-Electronic Activities?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was it who sent you to serve in that unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: In the 1992, for health reasons I left the combat units of the BiH Army. Towards the end of 1994 and the beginning of 1995, the military structures engaged me. They asked me to join that unit; to be more precise, to the element of that unit that was deployed on

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the necessary qualifications to carry out the tasks required from you in that unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Those are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer, Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd just like to request a redaction at line 17, just a location where the witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And, sorry, I also have another request. I think it's line 13. "1995" should be "1992." Sorry, page 13, lines 5 to 6. It should be -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should be perhaps -- this should be clarified perhaps again during the re-examination. I don't know if that was a mistake by translation or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, it's my mistake. It should be 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay, we leave it like this, and the other line will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Line 16 on page 13 will be redacted. Sorry for interrupting you, sir. Do you recall the question, the last question? Then please give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall the question. When I arrived at the southern site, I did not have the necessary qualifications. However, what we did mostly boiled down to the recording of conversations and their transcribing. I was not familiar with the technical part of the job, but I had enough knowledge to be able to record conversations and transcribe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While you were waiting to be deployed in that unit, did you undergo some intelligence and technical preparations which prepared you for work in that unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No intelligence education, and security education, that was required before you entered a unit of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and Mr. Tolimir not overlap, please, and could Mr. Tolimir please repeat his last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 5 of your statement, that you received the necessary information from the previous shift and from your commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did that information concern what happened on the ground or did it concern only the characteristics of the radio network that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: What do you mean by the events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say: "The commander of the previous shift provided us with the necessary information; for example, the frequencies used by the VRS." You mentioned only the frequencies. That's why I'm asking you whether they only provided you with the information about the frequencies on the radio frequencies, or did they provide you with the information about the activities on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: They provided us with the information on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down and don't overlap. Just wait, because the interpreters need a certain time to finish the translation. Now, please, your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most commonly, that was information about the currently active frequencies, the persons who were intercepted on those frequencies, the units working on those frequencies, and things like that. We did not receive much information from the front-line unless there were some activities going on. In that case, we would be informed about such activities going on in certain areas, and the frequencies that covered those areas had already been recorded and noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, how long did it take you to note a conversation which lasted, for example, three or five minutes? Usually, conversations take less than five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about longer conversations. Usually, the conversations were short, if my memory serves me well. I can't tell you how long it took me to transcribe, but let's say that a minute or two-minute-long conversation, I'm not 100 per cent sure, but it took me about 10 to 15 minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether in 10 or 15 minutes everything was completed and whether the conversation, the transcribed conversation, was ready to be sent off?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: It depended on the characteristics of the conversation. There were shorter conversations that lasted a minute or two. As for the priority of sending the transcribed conversations, that was decided by the unit commander. If the conversation that was recorded was very important, it was urgently transcribed and sent off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, how long were your shifts over one day, over 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: An active shift lasted 24 hours. You monitored frequencies over 24 hours, and then depending on the activities of that frequency, you worked for 24 hours. There were also night shifts, because during the day everybody was active, and during the night, there were people who were on duty who monitored certain frequencies if there were activities on such frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you: How long were you actively engaged and worked on the processing of conversations? I didn't ask you about duty service. I asked you about your active service.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: It depended on the activity on certain frequencies. That was what dictated our shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And in examination-in-chief, you said to the Prosecutor that the conversations that are compiled in the file were typed up over a period of 24 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: As far as I understood the question, the question was whether a conversation was usually typed up within the next 24 hours. We usually typed them up immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you typed them up immediately and handed them over to your commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did not type and code the conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Sometimes the operators did type the conversations up if they were short. I did it also a couple of times. But we did not have access to the code book. There were some cases when we typed up some shorter conversations if the main operator or the commander were absent. In their absence, we did it, but that wasn't a common occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you say when somebody else typed up your handwritten notes, did you then collate what you wrote in your hand and what somebody else subsequently typed up?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have to sign it?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at paragraph 6. We see it now. Under number 6 in your statement, you're talking about the procedures that you used when intercepting. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If something was not clear on the tape or if you became aware of a mistake that you had made, would you then cross out that word, would you replace it by a new word, or would you leave the word that you originally noted?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: We mostly used ballpoint pen, so we had to either cross the wrong word or we did not even record it if we were not absolutely certain that we had heard properly. If we were not certain that we heard properly, then we put the relevant word in brackets or we would just put three dots instead of any word that we were not sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you stated that you did not remember whether you knew anything about coding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Is it possible that you do not remember that you had any necessary knowledge or that you coded anything, and still that you do remember all the conversations that the Prosecutor asked you about on examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge that would allow me to code the reports. I don't remember ever having sent a single report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This may be a mistake. In the statement, it says: "I don't recall having knowledge required for coding."

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I don't remember that I ever coded any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I will read your statement back to you: "I don't remember whether I had any knowledge relative to coding."

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you do not remember that you had knowledge, not that you coded?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Well, it may be down to the style. In any case, nobody but the commander and the principal operator had access to the coding and the code book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you asked to subsequently collate your transcripts with the coded text?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No. In the most number of cases, the author of the text actually dictated his own text to the commander or to the main operator. We were there. We had an opportunity to observe what was being typed up. We were not asked to collate the two texts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see the third page of the statement in the Serbian language, and the English page that we see now can remain on the screen. We don't need to change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, in the last sentence, you say -- the following page is also in the English language, lines 7, 8, and 10 in paragraph 10: "While there are one or two other minor differences between the handwritten and typed versions, none of those differences change the meaning of the intercept." My question: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber and leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide whether there are differences and whether they change anything?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in these two or three reports, the information concerned Cerovic and whether he was colonel or lieutenant-colonel. In the handwritten version, it says "Colonel" or "Lieutenant-Colonel" in brackets. And as far as I can remember, in the typed-up material, the word is "Colonel." And I also noticed another discrepancy, if I may put it that way. In the place where the report refers to Krstic, X, and commander, the operator put a question mark next to the word "Mladic." In our report, we put it in brackets because we were familiar with the voice modulation, and from the context we could conclude that the person was, indeed, Commander Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what is in the handwritten version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Only "Mladic" without any question marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What other discrepancies have you noticed? You're talking about one or two minor differences?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: In document 2, it says "Colonel Cerovic," and then in brackets "Or Lieutenant-Colonel." In the printed version, it says "Colonel Cerovic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we scroll up the English version of the statement, and the Serbian version of the statement as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the screen, we now see that you signed only the English version of the statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I signed whatever they gave me to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that statement typed up in your presence, while you were being interviewed? Was the typist in the room or was it typed up subsequently?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 2007 case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You provided a statement on the 21st --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, 2007, and you can see it on the first page.

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I can see that, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You provided it to Mr. Thayer and Elderkin, and the interpreter was a woman, a Zlata?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was given this statement to review it and to sign it, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see your signature on the Serbian version or not, and whether you received it at the interview or not, and how long did it take to interview you?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: The January 2007 interview lasted for a single day before my evidence in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How many days did you spend at the Tribunal prior to testifying?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: One day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anyone speak to you before that?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Before what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before you arrived in The Hague. Did any Tribunal representatives speak to you in the federation?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer this: The statement you signed in English and in Serbian, were they both typed by two typists in your presence, while you were giving it, or was only the interpreter there?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I don't know whether they typed it up then. I only know I read it and confirmed its contents, and then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you able to read it immediately following the interview or did you wait for it to be typed up?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: Well, after it was typed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it wasn't during the interview?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't recall whether it was during the interview or immediately following it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In what language was the version you signed read back to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: In Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it was interpreted from English into Bosnian; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: It was translated into Bosnian, and as far as I recall, I signed it in English and in Bosnian. It was read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you signed it after it was read back to you, did you read the text yourself or did you read the English version?

utterances.speaker: PW-047
utterances.text: I don't speak English, and I signed the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. I would like to thank the witness for having provided answers here. I wish I was safe journey back, and God bless you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination, the evidence for today. Thank you very much for your attendance here in The Hague again, and you are free now to return to your home, to your normal activities. And the Chamber would like to thank you. The Court Officer will assist you. First, we have to close the screens again for your safety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: May I please be excused, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Have a nice day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He's ready, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then he should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please wait for a moment and stand. Good afternoon, sir, again. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You know protective measures are in place for you again, and first Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. As you know, my name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and I'm going to ask you just a few questions in relation to your evidence today. I just want to remind you to try and keep your voice up, and speak a little bit slowly, and allow some pause between questions and answers, so that the interpreters have a chance to translate accurately what you say, so that everyone can understand each other. Witness, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor against Vujadin Popovic on 12 December 2006?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your testimony truthful?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review your testimony or listen to your testimony before appearing in court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having done that, does your testimony fairly and accurately reflect what you would say if you were to be examined here today in this case?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just pause for a moment. I forgot something. Could I have the witness please shown P393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was waiting for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Please take a look at this sheet. See if you recognise your name. And without telling us -- without saying your name, can you confirm that you're the person named in relation to PW-041?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Having done that, Mr. President, I would like to offer into evidence P393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd also like to offer into evidence at this time P391 and P392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received as well, and the first under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that was dated 16 November 1999?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that statement before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you stand by that statement? Was it truthful and accurate as you gave it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer into evidence at this time the statement. It's P372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I would also like to offer into evidence -- actually, I'll proceed and I'll make an application to offer into evidence the intercepts in just a moment. Mr. President, I have a very brief summary in relation to the witness's evidence from the Popovic case that I'd like to read into the record. The witness adopted his OTP statement of 16 November 1999, which provided in substance as follows. If we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness worked at the northern facility throughout the rest of the war, following the orders and protocols of his command in the interception process. These procedures included scanning for and listening to radio communications, taping them, and then transcribing them manually into note-books. The transcription process sometimes required repeatedly replaying recorded conversations. Once a transcription was complete, the note-book entries were typed into a computer and encrypted. On occasion, the witness dictated his note-book entries to a typist, thus verifying its accuracy. The witness denoted portions of conversations that were inaudible by inserting ellipses into the relevant passages. In January 1996, the witness was demobilised. Per his testimony, the witness confirmed having obtained and transcribed 14 specific intercepts from July 1995. The witness noted that while he did not receive formal training as a member of the Interception Unit at the northern site, in addition to his JNA training which preceded his assignment there, he also received a Class B amateur radio certification in 1994. The witness recalled that there were generally two note-books in circulation during a shift, one used for current conversations and one to be used as needed. In addition, at least four UHER tape machines were available and in use in July 1995. The witness confirmed that during the interception process, transcribed conversations were reviewed as many as 20 times, if necessary, and then taken to a typist, where they were typed up, encrypted, and sent to the unit's command. He observed that generally the participants in the intercepted conversations tended to introduce themselves, almost as a standard practice. Sometimes their voices could be recognised with certainty. However, where participants or passages in the intercepted conversations could not be determined with 100 per cent certainty, question marks or parentheses were used to reflect this. In addition, where the participants could not be determined, an X or Y would be used. That concludes my summary, and I have just a few additional questions. I would like to have this booklet handed over to the witness so he can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, you have a booklet there of some 19 intercepts. Let me ask you: Were you shown this booklet prior to having testified here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the handwritten note-book transcriptions that are contained in it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in addition to that, did you have an opportunity -- a previous opportunity to review the original note-books from which those photocopies of the handwritten transcriptions were taken?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the 19 intercepts that are contained in the booklet were written down by you?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were they transcribed by you during the course and scope of your duties and responsibilities as an intercept operator on or about the date that the conversations actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to compare the handwritten intercepts -- your handwritten transcriptions against certain print-out or printed-out transcriptions?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the printed-out transcriptions in the booklet that you have there of 19 intercepts correspond to the handwritten entries that you made in the note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, I would offer into evidence all 19 intercepts, 14 of which came in through the witness's prior testimony and 5 of which are new. I can give you the numbers of them, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please indicate and, for the record, tell the first and the last number of this package of transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, not transcripts, but exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibits are P373A and B through P385. All right. And then I have -- no, through P386. I'm sorry. And then I have P394 through P398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, but I would like to note that P269D is already an exhibit admitted through another witness on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I think also P386 seems to have another number as well, as P0015.1 and .2. I think those came in pursuant to a 92 quater application, but I see here it also has been pre-marked as P386. So just so the record is clear that they're one and the same, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have a present recollection of the 19 intercepts that are contained in the booklet before you?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you about is some of the -- a little bit about the process of interception as occurred in the northern facility. Now, per your prior statement, you indicated that part of the job of interception required that you scan certain frequencies. Can you tell us who determined what frequencies were scanned by the operators?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The operators searched by way of radio-relay equipment, the 800 sets. This is what we had. And we also had an FM 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you told what specific range of frequencies or specific frequencies to search for, or was it simply up to the operators to determine what they would be searching for?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We received instructions about what directions to take, in terms of turning our antennae in that direction, and then after that it was easy to find a channel or a frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And without giving us any names, can you tell us whom you received these instructions from? Would it be a squad commander or a platoon commander or company commander?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We received instructions from our squad commander, who probably received his commands from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of the process of intercepting, was that overseen by anyone?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Of course it was. The squad commander was always with us. He even assisted at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did the squad commander review entries that you made in the note-books or that the operators made in the note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: He frequently did, but he wasn't physically present at all times when we did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As an intercept operator, from your statement, you didn't receive any formal training on how to do your job, but did you receive any training in general as to how to do it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We all learned as we went. The only formal training was the Ham Radio classification I received. As for the rest, we gained experience under our commander as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the other operators that you worked with also had earned Ham Radio certifications?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few of them. At the beginning of the war, most of my work-mates had been Ham Radio enthusiasts. We all worked together, and we joined the unit to do our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the manual transcription, that is, the writing down of these conversations into the note-book, once that was completed you said that it was taken to a typist. Do you know what the typist did with that material?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: He would take our handwritten transcripts, and this person was a communications person who would type things up and encrypt the conversations. Then all that would be sent by way of Paket communication to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was anybody -- or, that is, any operator permitted to type and encrypt intercepted communications and send them over to the command, or was that limited in some way?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: In my squad, we had a designated person who worked on that. He had undergone special training for that. We weren't familiar with the encryption systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the course of transcribing an intercept, did you on occasion work with other members of your unit in order to determine what can be heard on a tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In situations in which, for example, I could not make out a word in a sentence, then I asked for their assistance. I also asked for their assistance in terms of deciding who the interlocutors are, since by that time we were able to recognise most of them by the tone of their voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you permitted, as an operator, to write down a participant or interlocutor's name into the intercept based solely upon recognising that speaker's voice?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to write down a person's name as a speaker in a definitive sense based solely upon your recognition of the tone of their voice or their manner of speaking?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, but frequently they also introduced themselves at the opening, which was further corroboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you recognised a person's voice, would you denote that in the intercept in some way, as distinguished from when a person is introduced or when their name was actually mentioned in the recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So can you tell us how it's possible to tell the difference between whether or not a person's name was spoken during an intercept, intercepted communication, or whether or not you simply -- an intercept operator simply recognised their name? Is there a way to tell the difference in -- in what's written down in the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: In some conversations, you can see for yourself that they introduced themselves, and then in others it is absent. However, we listened to them on a daily basis, and for the most part we didn't need their introductions. We immediately knew who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would you write that down in the print-out or you wouldn't write that down at all?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in some instances a name can appear as a speaker in a print-out, although the person's name isn't mentioned in the text of the conversation. Is that the case or would that be the case if a person's name were spoken before the tape-recorder were turned on?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber, how that could occur?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: At the beginning of a conversation, it could happen that those at the switchboard who had to put people through would be contacted, and people required them to be put through to a certain person, and at the very outset such people would introduce themselves. This first, initial part of the conversation usually did not have anything of particular interest. We listened to the conversations, themselves. However, a recording is made of the totality of a conversation, whereas I only noted down those portions which I believed were interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so would it be the case that in certain conversations that you noted down, the speaker may not be referred to expressly in the conversation, even if you noted down their name as being a participant?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: It had to be introduced at the beginning of the conversation or I had to recognise the voice. I didn't do it in any random way, arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when that occurred, did you note down the person's name at the time that you listened to the conversation on any piece of paper, or in the note-book, or any place else before you actually later did the transcription from the tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, you see, any conversation was recorded from the very beginning, and then when we rewound the tape, we introduced the participants as we recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was a little unclear. Let me try a different way. When you had a conversation where the person's name isn't mentioned and you don't recognise the voice, but the person was introduced before you turned on the tape-recorder, did you note down that name at the time that you heard it or did you note it down at some other time?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: If I did not hear the name, I would use an X/Y designation. If I didn't recognise the participant or if the participant wasn't introduced, there was no place for speculation there. What you heard is what you noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to try one more time. When you recorded a conversation and the introduction was not recorded, did you write down the person who was introduced at the time you turned on the recorder or did you write it down at some point later?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I'm not able to answer your question. I don't know. There are very few and far between situations like that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, when you listen to a tape-recorder and the person wasn't introduced, how did you know who was speaking if they introduced themselves and you didn't record it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that -- I still don't understand your question. I'm not sure what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you sometimes not get the person's name on the tape-recorder before you started taping? Let's start there.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you didn't get the person's name on the tape-recorder and you later transcribed what was on the tape-recorder, did you make a note at the time that you turn on the tape-recorder who was speaking so that you can recall later who is on the recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Okay. When a conversation started and when we started recording, at that same moment we were duty-bound to record the time, the frequency, and the participants in the conversation, and the UHER equipments were reset back to zero to indicate when the conversation started. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you write down the participants of the conversation at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that how you were able to recall who the participants were for a given conversation when you later transcribed it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From that piece of paper, is that what's transferred and written into the note-books; frequency, date, time, participants, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's what's -- is that what's also given over to the typist and put in the typed-out version of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The typist received my note-book. When my shift was over, I handed the note-book over to him, unless there was an urgency and something needed to be typed before my shift was over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that perhaps a convenient time for the first break? Then you have the opportunity to think about certain -- rephrasing of some questions to make something more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If there are some questions you'd like me to ask. I really only have one more or two more questions that I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to mention, very shortly, we have received several documents you tendered, but three of them don't have an English translation yet. These are P375B, P382B, and P398B. These three will only be marked for identification, pending translation. We must have the first break now, on technical reasons, and we will adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you about the piece of paper that you write down certain information on before you actually transcribe a conversation into your note-book. Once you've transcribed -- or once you've put the information on the piece of paper into your note-book, what happens to the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We would leave such papers aside. The commander was there. I don't know what happened to them. But as far as I'm concerned, I would usually note everything in my note-book immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in your packet of 19 intercepts here, there are a couple of instances in which a Tolimir is mentioned by name; not as a speaker, per se, but is in the intercept, itself. Do you know whether or not or can you recall whether or not those entries concerning Tolimir refer to General Tolimir of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, the answer wasn't recorded on the record. Would you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It won't go on. It's flashing -- all right. Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have, please, in e-court -- I'd like to show the witness P395. I believe it's tab 11 in the booklet. It will be 395A, I think is the handwritten. This should be -- yes, this is an intercept that is dated 18 July, and the time is 1831.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular conversation, you can see that there's a reference to Tolimir, and it's probably about the fifth line down or the fifth entry down, which reads that: "He is the first on the list, that the approval came from Tolimir and they will try tomorrow or most likely the day after tomorrow." Do you see that in the handwritten version?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the reference to Tolimir in this case, would that be something that you would have heard on the tape, as opposed to something that you would have deduced from the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: This was taken from the tape. I didn't deduce this. We never deduced anything. What we heard on the tape was subsequently transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P384, please, and that should be tab 14 in this packet of 19 intercepts. And I'd like to show you A, P34A, that's in the packet again -- P384A. Okay, I think we have it up on the screen. This is an intercept that's dated 21st July 1995. It's at 1030. And in the English version, it looks about 10 lines from the bottom of the screen, you can see it reads: "But he has a meeting scheduled with our side and the military side from that hole down there." "D," Djurcic in this case, says: "Yes, yes. "L," Lelek: "But General Tolimir told me this morning not to let anyone go up there." Further down you can see: "And when did General Tolimir tell you this?" And repeats General Tolimir's name one more time after that. Would that be also something that you would have heard definitively on the tape as opposed to something you might have or could have deduced from the nature of the conversation? Just so that you know, the references to Tolimir can be found at the bottom of the page ending 1 -- 513 in B/C/S, and in the middle of -- the top and the middle of the page, of the following, of the following page, 514.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Again, this is another conversation from a tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to refer you, if I can, to 513, which is still on the screen here, where you have "Lelek," and then written in parentheses you have what appears to be "Domar." And then following that you have "Puk Djurcic." Can you tell us why you have "Domar" written in parentheses?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The first participant, Lelek, and in brackets this is the name for the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that something mentioned in the tape-recording or is that some other information that you had?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: There's no other source. The recording on the tape is the only source we relied on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of performing your job as an intercept operator, were certain aids made available to you, such as information from your commanders, maps, code-names, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, we had maps, our commander provided us with information, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were the maps pertinent to locations, people, frequencies, things of that nature? Can you tell us what they were -- what they concerned, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: What I can remember is the fact that the maps depicted the names of the switchboards.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to use those or rely on those in transcribing intercepts or writing down certain information concerning those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: They didn't mean much to me, particularly. When I transcribed my conversations, I just transcribed my conversations. Those maps were much more important for my commander. In my case, I tried to make sure that I transcribed the conversations that I heard as accurately as I heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How important was it that your transcriptions accurately reflected what was on the tape?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: That was the most important thing. We tried very hard to make those transcripts as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, do you have questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everybody once again, and I would like to greet the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since we speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a five-second pause after the end of my question to avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P372, P372. This is the statement provided by the witness to the OTP on the 16th of November, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Before the 16th of November, were you in touch with anybody from the OTP and from this Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Can I now start answering?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. After I say, Thank you, you can start answering.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Do you mean before I provided my statement, whether I had any contacts with anybody from the Tribunal? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having been in touch with anybody before I provided my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what about after you provided the statement, did you have any contacts with the personnel of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber when and where? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but I know that we were invited to come to the command of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, and a representative of the Tribunal was there to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who invited you and whether you were there all together or just you, yourself? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I can't tell you who invited me because I don't remember. Several people had been invited, and while I provided my statement, I was on my own in the room together with the official of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, when was that, what year and what month? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was after the testimony provided on the 16th of November, 1999, and before your appearance in court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did not testify in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you provided your statement on the 16th of November, 1999. Where was that, in the federation or here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: In the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And after that, after you provided your statement, did you testify in the Popovic case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will repeat. You provided your statement to the OTP on the 16th of November, 1999, and that statement was used in the Popovic case; is that the case, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that -- actually, how much time elapsed between the time you provided your statement and your first testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: My first testimony happened in 2003, but not in the case that you mentioned a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that here at the Tribunal or did you testify before a national court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide any other statement before that or did you testify about the same circumstances you are testifying about today? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, between the 16 November 1999 and the testimony in 2003, did you get in touch with any of those persons?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: What persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You now said that you do not remember when you got in touch with the representatives of the Tribunal. Was that during the period between 1999 and 2003? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: As I told you, in 1999 I provided my statement. My first testimony here at the Tribunal was in 2003. And after that, I testified once again two and a half years ago here, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide another statement before the testimony in 2003? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't know what statement you're talking about. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During that testimony, were you shown a statement? Had the Trial Chamber been provided with a statement? Did the OTP have the statement? Did the accused have a statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: At all times, they used this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So what did you testify about in 2003, and what did you talk about with the OTP between 1999 and 2003? What did you discuss and when?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: In 2003, I testified here at this Tribunal, and that was that. And you mean after the statement that I provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you, thank you. In which case did you testify in 2003? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The Jokic and Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you testify -- or did you base your testimony on the same statement that we are discussing here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you use the same transcripts that we're using here today? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I can't answer that, because in the previous cases we used some conversations, but I don't remember which ones of those that we are looking at here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And after 2003, did you have any more contacts with the representatives of the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The next time after that was when I came here two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that in the Popovic case? The Prosecutor mentioned that on the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in all the cases, the same statement was used, the one that we are using here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you need to seek approval from the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina to appear at the Tribunal and to talk to the representatives of the Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I just needed an approval for a leave of absence from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How many persons were present while you provided your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were two people present, just as it is indicated on the first page; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which of the two persons typed your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, I did not pay any attention to that. I know both persons. I remember when they visited me. Which one of them was typing, I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they have a laptop or a typewriter on the desk while they were talking to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, they had a laptop and a printer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you then given your statement to sign? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement in your own language or in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can't answer, could you please look at the screen in front of you and tell us in which language is the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How come you did not sign a statement in your own mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you speak English, since you signed the statement in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: A little.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge of English, were you able to sign the statement after having read it yourself or was it read to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The statement was read back to you 100 per cent accurately, loud and clear, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At that time, you were not given a version in your own mother tongue, only in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown page 2 in the same document, and please zoom in on paragraph 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are looking at paragraph 4, where it says that: "In April 1992, I, together with four or five other amateur radio enthusiasts, linked together and joined the Territorial Defence Unit (TDU) as radio interceptors. We initially used our own equipment. Some time later we were given relatively modern equipment." My question is this: How did you join the Territorial Defence Unit? Was that after a conversation with somebody? Did somebody prepare you for that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, a former officer of the JNA talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At that time, was he a member of the JNA or the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Before the war, he was a JNA officer. And when the war started, he joined the BiH Army and worked for the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then receive paperwork to regulate your status with the Territorial Defence or the BiH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, we received the paperwork. I can't tell you exactly what that was, but at first we were given Territorial Defence booklets and then they were BiH Army booklets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does your military booklet reflect the date when you joined the Territorial Defence, and was that later used towards your pensionable years?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, what equipment did you have, your own equipment, for interception?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
