utterances.text: We had Radio Ham stations, and as far as I can remember, we also received -- is it really important for me to give you the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is important, because you stated that they were later on transported to the northern site. I would be interested to know what you used to intercept those conversations.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We had those -- I don't know where they came from, but they were called RUP. And when we were transferred -- or, rather, that was at the first location. And then the second group that came from Banovici, they brought the receivers that we used. They were of a rather good quality. Those were ICOM IC-7000A R-3000 equipment, and then those that we called hundreds, the broadband type of equipment for interception for a broad range of frequencies that could be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please explain for the Trial Chamber, when you say "hundreds," what do you mean? What kind of equipment was that?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: That was a radio receiver. I can't remember the frequencies that it could intercept, but in any case we used them to -- for the frequencies of 200 megahertz, and as well as radio-relay equipment that we used the most, the radio-relay equipment 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you get this, as you call it, relatively up-to-date equipment, that is, the last sentence of the fourth paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: It was at the very beginning, in the summer, I think. The equipment was brought by our Ham Radio operators from Banovici and Tuzla. I don't know where they got it, but it was a relatively new equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of equipment it was so that we would be aware of what means you used to gather information?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: These were radio receiver sets. They couldn't transmit. They were specifically designed to receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you modify any of those radio receivers? Did you work on them or did you use them in their original form as received, since you cannot remember which ones those specifically are?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I think I told you which ones those are. The only modification was with the RRU 800. We simply created converters, small pieces of equipment which split the 24 channels to further sets from the original receiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, there's no need to be upset. You only said "receivers," but you did not specifically name the type.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you also adapt the antennae you had for your receivers to suit your needs better?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I didn't do that personally. I was an operator. But our commanders were fully versed in that field, and they could place well-directed antennae which fully met our needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 in your statement - do you see it? - in the Serbian it's page 2, you say: "While we were at Lipik, on Mount Majevica ..." And there is mention of the autumn of 1993. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, Lipik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say that until the fall of 1993, you noted conversations down on pieces of paper available, and I quote: "The majority of the conversations, however, were dictated directly from the reel-to-reel tapes to the typist and then transmitted to the 2nd Corps headquarters." Did I accurately quote your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you clarify for the Chamber what you say in paragraph 5, something you describe as standard procedure, that it was dictated directly from reel-to-reel tapes to the typists so that there was no need for you to take handwritten notes? Why was it done this way?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I can explain that quite simply. It was 1993. This was at Lipik, on Mount Majevica. At the very beginning, we were completely isolated and we made do with what we had. We noted conversations down on whatever paper was available. Quite a few of those conversations were sent directly by phone, and later on received computers, and we used Paket communication. (redacted), where we were joined by the other group, and things were much better organised then, making it far easier to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that it was dictated to the typist. Would the typist type it into a computer or did they use typewriters?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: They typed it into computers. Urgent conversations could also have been transmitted by phone, before the use of Paket communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Vanderpuye, I think everybody's noticed that there was a name mentioned which should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 51, line 18, especially. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement you say as follows, and you can check the accuracy: "In October 1993, this radio-intercept operation was transferred to" the northern site. My question is this: Did you move all of the equipment from Lipik to the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any units remain at Lipik or was the location shut down?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I think only the sentry unit remained. They trained their young recruits there. We left our facility, however, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you moved to the northern site, did you continue with this practice of dictating directly from the tapes to the typist?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: No. By that time, we had a person who encrypted the conversations, and he was the only person with access to that computer. It was our task to bring all our note-books, once our shift was finished, to him, and then he sent it on to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the northern site, did you have an antenna system?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had antenna systems. Each set that needed its own antenna had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So there was no need for you to use the old antennae you had brought from Lipik; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, let me explain something. We did not use the radar systems of the JNA because they took all of it away. In the meantime, our commanders made some more equipment, and it was all enough for us to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to know this: Did you use the old antenna systems you had at Lipik with your equipment or did you make use of any other antennae?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, we had this new equipment. Some of it was from before, and we also received new sets. They were new, in terms of production, and we made our antennae.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you had sets without antennae; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Without any antenna systems, we would not have been able to intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But the new sets which you received, did they have their own antenna systems or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: They did, but these were our antenna systems. We did not receive original antennae. It was our commanders who created these antenna systems for us, and that is what we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you move those antennae, did you change their positions or direction, depending on the participants and frequencies of a particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We turned our antennae in the direction it was ordered to us. If the direction was the Drina Corps, that is the angle at which we would place the antennae. You know very well that once radio-relay equipment is mounted, it is stationary. You turn your antenna in a certain direction where the signal is the strongest, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. But there was some mention made here of some primitive means being used, but I don't think this is the way you had to resort to.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: No, we had a relatively new, modern equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also have an expert -- a technical expert who was charged with mounting and maintaining those systems?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I think I said that at the beginning. All of us were enthusiasts, radio amateurs with experience. There were technical engineers among us, so we did not have any technical problems in that sense. I remember very few problems, breakdowns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there a single person, out of the number of experts you had there, who was tasked with maintaining and setting up the antennae and radio receivers, or was it done by several people?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Once those antenna systems are set up, they work, and there's nothing there to be meddled with unless they had to be redirected. But as far as I know, I can remember very few instances when something needed to be repaired. In any case, these people were always available and ready to assist, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how far removed were the antennae from the receivers, themselves?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Some antennae were up on the roof, so quite close; whereas some antenna systems were on a nearby hill, close to the room where we worked in the PPS, so the distance was at least 10 metres in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you on duty 'round the clock for the 15 days referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: No, not 'round the clock. That would have been impossible. Our practice was to be on duty three to four hours, unless there was significant activity, and then it would take us longer to rewind the tapes and do everything that was necessary. But not 'round the clock. That would not have been feasible. You cannot work for 24 hours like that. We would do our shift, and then we're ready to assist, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, in paragraph 1, you say that your shift lasted 15 days, and then you would be on leave the next 15 days. That is why I asked you whether you were on duty 'round the clock for the 15 days in question. How long did an operator sit to process the conversations in his shift?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, three to four hours, unless we needed more time. For the 15 days, we were there, and then we rotated. However, the equipment was on non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is why I'm asking you that. I asked you how long you, as operators, worked in a period of 24 hours. Let's take you, for example.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely, but it would be three to four days -- three to four hours, unless there was more activity. In the evening, there would be less activity, and only one person remained on duty. There was no need for two or three of us to be awake throughout the night. And, of course, in the morning, at around 5.00, we would wake up, but the system was well worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 3, as you can see, on page 3, you say in the first sentence: "We used the scanning function on our equipment." Does that mean that when a certain set has the scanning ability, there was no need to do anything manually or to move the antennae?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: You are quite right in that, but this has nothing to do with the antennae. These were state-of-the-art sets. Once a conversation was on, the scanning was stopped, the UHER recorder would turn on, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any special instruction on how to work with the equipment or did you receive any instruction on the activities of the units you monitored?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Any information and orders were conveyed to us by our commander. We followed his instructions, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4 - you can follow it there to see whether I'm quoting accurately - it says: "Everything was recorded, and we would only note down the frequencies, dates, and names on a piece of paper." My question is this: Did you also -- did you only note down the frequencies, date, time, and names, whereas the rest was unimportant, or was it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, I have just started to explain that. The set would register a conversation. The scanning function would be stopped and the UHER recorder turned on. As the recording went on, we noted down the time, frequency, and the rest. Once the conversation was finished, the recording would be stopped and the scanner turned on. If something was urgent, in our assessment, we would start transcribing immediately, and then a work-mate would sit down at the set and continue working. So, things went smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any need to burn any documents or use them for other purposes out of the transcripts you made by hand?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I never burned my transcripts, and I didn't see anyone else do so. Once I used up a note-book, I would hand it over to the commander, and he would be better placed to tell you what he did with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this closes the topic of papers. You handed them over to your commander. What about the tapes; what was done with them by you, the operators, once they were filled?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Once the tape reached its end, we did the same thing we used to do with the note-books. I would hand it over, put in a fresh tape, and the commander used the old ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever re-record a single tape? Did you ever tape another conversation over a previous one?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: That is quite likely, because when the commander returned tapes to us, I didn't know whether it was an old tape which was erased or not. We seldom had fully new tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have a set of equipment which could have been used solely for erasing at that location?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 of your statement - it's the last paragraph on page 3 - you say that you compared -- I quote: "I did not have much contact with them, but from time to time when I could hear a piece of conversation, I would compare that to the material collected by the State Security Service. That way, occasionally we managed to see both ends of the line." Can you explain to the Chamber whether you could determine both participants, based on that portion of the conversation, or were you able to establish what both of the services gathering such information were doing?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Well, this is a number of questions. It's confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that first you heard one participant, and then based on what the State Security recorded, you made your comparisons and then you could gain information about both participants. Are you referring to both services that intercepted the conversations or both participants in the conversation that you monitored?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Most probably, although as far as I can remember, of course, that we shared the same facility for a while and we had some contacts, of course, but I never followed -- we never knew what they were monitoring. I believe -- after such a long time, I can't really remember, but I believe that it did happen, that I could hear one participant in a conversation and I couldn't hear the other at all. It didn't happen often, but I can't exclude such a possibility. It was probably within that context that I stated that. I did ask them whether they were monitoring the same conversation, whether they recorded it, and whether they could assist me with deciphering who the other participant was. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that reliable? If you heard only one part of the conversation, was that enough for you to compare what you had and what the other service had, what they had recorded? Was that enough for you to conclude who the second participant was, if you could not conclude that based on your intercept alone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: We cannot talk about any deductions or drawing conclusions. We are talking about entire conversations when I could only hear one participant in the conversation. At the same time, the identical -- the same conversation was recorded by them. I don't know whether you have had an occasion to hear any such intercepted conversations. There's no place for deductions. The conversations recorded by one service and by the other are absolutely identical, and there's no room for guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to you. I'm only reading from your statement. I'm quoting your words in the fifth paragraph, in the last two sentences. You can check, if you want. However, you just told us that it was very rarely that you could hear only one participant. Did I understand you properly? Is that why it wasn't necessary for you to ask for their assistance, because such situations were few and far between? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that in the conversations that you were listening to, you could hear the interlocutor in Sarajevo as well as the one in Han Pijesak, for example? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown page 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The first sentence on page 4, which you see already, reads: "When we identified the frequencies, we used the working map on the wall of the room where we worked." My question is this: Was that map always the same or was it changed? Was it changed often? How was it drawn, who drew it up? What information it contained? Did it contain all the information that the Ham operators needed or, rather, the intercept operators needed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: It says here when we identified frequencies, that means that we used that map, and what I meant by that was the fact that the map allowed me to determine the direction from which the signal came. It was the commander who used the map most often. He inserted the names of the participants and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know how the maps are drawn. Can you please tell me whether it was often changed or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: The map, as such, there was just one, as far as I can remember. And as for what he drew on it, what he inserted on it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In any case, you always saw just one map that you used to define the elements that you could then use on your equipment. Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you recorded only conversations involving the VRS or whether you also recorded conversations of the units for which you provided intelligence support, because that's why your unit is called the Electronics Support Unit or the Unit for Electronic Warfare? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: I personally monitored what was ordered to me by the commander. Those were predominantly officers of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you monitor anybody else or anything else but the VRS officers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, only them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember any other conversation, save for the 19 that are before you in the file? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Sir, there were so many conversations, I don't even know their number. You're asking me to try and recall a conversation now. It's a very tall order. It would be very difficult for me to remember any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It would be difficult to remember even the 19 that are before us if you didn't have the transcript before you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you stated that you had used a BC 91 and 42; pages 35 and 36 and 91. Are those only the note-book pages which contain the transcripts that are today before you?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Could you please assist me? Could you please help me? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before you is a file with 19 conversations under 19 different numbers?

utterances.speaker: PW-041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question of the witness. Do you have any problems and need a break? That was the impression some people formed. If you need a break, just indicate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, we should have the second break now, and we will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes, I need a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. We will have the second break now, and we will resume 10 minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are in a problematic situation because the health condition of the witness is not the best and he can't continue the hearing and giving evidence this afternoon, so that we are facing a problem. The next hearing will be next week, on Tuesday. The witness -- if we continue examining this witness, he has to stay over the weekend, and we have to resume on Tuesday with this witness, if he is then able and he is in a better health condition. The other option could be to have an additional hearing tomorrow just to finish this witness so that we could give him the opportunity to travel back to his home, if his health condition is better tomorrow. We have no indication for that, but we should think about that, if we could be quite flexible. Mr. Tolimir, could you give us an estimation, how much additional time you need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If the witness is sick and if he has to travel where he can be treated, I agree that he should be sent straight away. And as for my questioning, if I don't put all of my questions, it will not change my destiny, I will not be acquitted or convicted. May God be of assistance to this witness, and may he make him feel better. We will pray for him. As far as I'm concerned, I wish him the best of health, and you do what is best for the witness. As far as I am concerned, you do whatever you, as the Trial Chamber, deem to be the best for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are very nice words. On the other hand, Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any misunderstanding, you are not under time pressure. You have the right to continue your cross-examination. It's up to you to decide. If you have additional questions and if you want to use the time perhaps in an additional hearing tomorrow or next week, or if you say it is not so important, you have had the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, this is only up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let your decision be appropriate to the witness's health. I'm sure that his sojourn here until next Tuesday would not be beneficial for him. If you think that he should stay until Tuesday, then I'm prepared to give up on all the questions that I may still have had for him. If you think that he can appear tomorrow, then I am prepared to put a few more questions to him. Thank you very much. I appreciate your understanding. I know that you want to do best by the witness, by myself, and by the OTP, although I believe that the OTP does not have any additional questions for the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your position. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Tolimir is right. I don't have any additional questions for this witness as a result of the examination so far. But I do want to stress, because I think it's important, that we do not wish to put Mr. Tolimir in a position where he is required to waive his right of cross-examination of this witness, given the fact that we've presented the evidence of this witness. And although he's willing and flexible, in terms of the cross-examination or how much additional cross-examination he may have, I just want the record to be clear that we're not requesting that, and if he wants to do that, that's certainly his prerogative, but I just want that to be clear. We have two witnesses that we're able to go with, I think, today, one of which I think can probably be finished today. It might be a good idea to proceed with them, or at least the one, and then find out if it's suitable for the witness, who has taken ill, if he's able or willing to continue next week. And if that's possible, then I think that's probably a pretty good solution. That way, Mr. Tolimir can reflect on whether he wishes to further examine the witness, and hopefully the witness will be in a good-enough shape at that time to proceed and complete, I think, a relatively short portion or remaining examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this position. It's the position of the Chamber as well. There should be no time restraint for Mr. Tolimir. Before we entered the court, I asked Madam Registrar to find out the situation of the witness during the last hour of our hearing this afternoon, and I hope we have some more additional information before we adjourn this evening. I think it's a good proposal to continue with the next witness. And this one will be which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's PW-038, Witness 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I be excused for the rest of the proceedings, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it is inhumane to force the witness to stay here ill over the weekend because of a few additional questions. I am ready to conclude my examination. Mr. Vanderpuye is right in what he says, but I waive my right, and there's nothing problematic about this particular witness. There is no mention of my name or myself in these intercepts alone. Therefore, it is not essential for me to continue. Given that he is ill, he should be released to go home. Pressure is a very difficult thing for those who are unaccustomed to it, especially when they are in completely new circumstances such as these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber appreciates your position, and we should consider what you have said. We should make a decision at the end of today's hearing. Good afternoon, Mr. Elderkin. The next witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. I will be examining the next witness, and I'd like to state for the record the witness has the protective measures of pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please wait a moment so that the screens are opened. Again, good afternoon. Could you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, for the Prosecution, has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. As you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin. And just before I start asking questions, I want to remind you to try to keep your voice up and speak into the microphones, and to speak slowly enough for the interpreters to translate between what we're saying. And if there's any question that I ask you that is unclear, then please say so, and I will do my best to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please, could I ask for 65 ter 6297 to be shown, and that's marked as P416.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, please, could you look at what's written on the screen, and without reading it aloud, can you confirm if that is your name?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask for the pseudonym sheet to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, under seal, with the given number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying here in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to listen to that testimony in your language yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does your testimony from 2007 fairly, accurately, and truthfully reflect what you would say if you were asked the same questions in court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: In essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd move, Your Honours, to have the 2007 testimony admitted. It's as P414, which is the confidential version under seal, and the public version is P415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd also request at this time, Your Honours, for the admission of the witness's May 1999 witness statement, which was the basis of his evidence in the Popovic case and an exhibit to his evidence in that case, which is P406, also to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: With your permission, I'd now like to read a very short summary of the witness's evidence, and this can all be open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The witness was a member of the BiH Army. In July 1995, he was an intercept operator, based at the northern location. His work practice followed the established procedure of scanning, recording, and transcribing intercepts into note-books. Normal practice was to work in six-hour shifts, followed by a six-hour break, depending on how busy it was. During the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, people worked for 20 hours a day. The intercept operators grew to know which channels to monitor on particular frequencies, and became skilled at identifying many of the voices they heard. The witness was able to recognise several VRS officers' voices and knew several VRS code-names. That concludes my summary, and I have, with the Court's permission, a few additional questions for the witness. I'd ask the Usher could pass up a packet of intercepts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday did you have a chance to review this file containing 11 intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you also see yesterday the original handwritten note-books in which you originally recorded those conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do the intercepts in the blue file before you correspond with those original note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are the intercepts in the file on your desk now the copies of intercepts that you saw in the original note-books yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the intercepts at all 11 tabs in the blue file are in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you listen to, record, and transcribe those intercepts in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Generally, how soon after intercepting a conversation did you transcribe it into a note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: It all depended on the importance and urgency of a conversation. It was done either immediately or 10 to 20 minutes later. In any case, first it was all recorded and then subsequently noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And is that true specifically of these 11 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I'm not certain for all of them, but most of it was taken down and transcribed within such a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you also look yesterday at printed versions of those intercepts in the file?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do the handwritten intercepts correspond with the printed versions that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At this time, I'd ask to have the 11 intercepts admitted as indicated on the tender list. And the first seven of the intercepts in the packet, which are P407, 408, 409, 410, 411, 412, and 413, were all admitted through this witness in the Popovic trial, and P417, 418, 419, and P420 were not used with or admitted through this witness in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first set of documents will be received, but the Exhibit numbers P407B, C and D only marked for identification, pending translation. And could you please indicate if the second set of documents are contained in the binder of 11 intercepts we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, they are at tabs 8 through 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. These four intercepts will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And, Witness, thank you. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Witness, now the accused has the right to put questions to you in his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet all those present yet again, including the witness. I hope today's testimony will be concluded following God's will and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, after my questions, please pause shortly so as not to overlap. Otherwise, your answers will not make part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: First, I'd like for your witness statement to be shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P406. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the cover page in English. Could we have both cover pages on the screen at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In what language did you sign your statement, what version?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The Bosnian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the English version being signed, and your mother-tongue version is not signed. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I can, but I signed the English version which was read back to me in Bosnian, although I don't know why there is no signature on the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Save for those two persons whose names we can see on the cover page, were there any other persons present? It seems that one of these people interviewed you and the other one interpreted.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, these were the two people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they record your interview?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was or not. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which one of these two typed up the conversation, and in what language?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a question to ask. Can I freely mention any names? Can I mention the name of the person working on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the names of the persons who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is no problem. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the names of the language staff, our practice is to request that it's in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it was in English and that it was interpreted to me into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it was interpreted to you orally, whereas she typed it up in English?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: They showed me the Bosnian version as well, and they told me what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could they have typed it up immediately in both languages?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't think it was done simultaneously. I think one version preceded the other. Otherwise, I would not have signed the English version, since I do not understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see on the screen that you did sign the English version, whereas you did not sign the version in your mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Which version did he sign, the English or his mother-tongue version?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The statement before me has my signature in the English version. I know what it's about because it was put to me in Bosnian as well, and I do not have an explanation for why it was not signed in Bosnian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to another topic. You provided this statement in 1999. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: In Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that, did anyone speak to you from the Tribunal about any statements and material presented in proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Before that, I had had no contact with any Tribunal representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have any following contacts with OTP representatives?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it was in 1999 onwards. It all took place in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did it have to do with this particular statement or did it have to do with something else?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: It had to do with this statement as well as some other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did those cases have to do with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you also provide certain statements concerning Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you provide another statement, in addition to this one, that would have to do with the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: This is the only statement I gave, and it had to do with the rest of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it contain any descriptions of those events because of which you were contacted by Tribunal representatives?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: As far as I can see here before me, it does not, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what the topic of that discussion was, since it was not in the material forwarded to us?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: When I gave the statement, all of this information, well, the gist -- well, this is the statement, these were the questions they put, and I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you also signed the information you provided to them?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, according to what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were any other people included in the process?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: No, the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please explain, in your own words, why did those persons again contact you, and when was that, and was it in Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please not answer this question in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have just one more question about this topic. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, the part of the statement that you subsequently signed and that was used in the previous cases, can that be considered a secret agreement or can that part also be made public as well as this one? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have just told us that in the repeated contacts with the same persons, you provided several statements for the cases in which you previously testified. Those statements are not here today. That's why I'm asking you whether those statements contained some sort of agreement between you and those persons that are not supposed to be made public, which are secret.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: No, sir, the same statement. Whenever I testified, we only used one sentence -- one and only statement that I provided and that I used in my testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just told us that you even signed something after those repeated conversations and contacts. What was that?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Only an affidavit that there was, indeed, a conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Never mind, let's move on to another group of questions. I don't want to waste any more time. Let's move on to something easier. In the third paragraph of your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the page where -- with the third paragraph? Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the third paragraph, in the first sentence, you said: "I joined the BH Army in March 1993, and I was deployed to a unit for radio surveillance"?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please explain, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and for my own benefit, what does this mean? What is the meaning of "electronic reconnaissance"? Did you perform electronic reconnaissance, and what pieces of equipment did you use for electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I apologise. Could we again go into private session? I can't provide my answers in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 3 of this document - could it be displayed, please - in paragraph 3 you say, in the last sentence: "I had the discretion to decide what was and what was not important." And in the second line of the same paragraph, you say that you made only brief summaries. Could you please explain what was entered in those brief summaries and what did you mean when you say that you had the discretion to decide?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: As an operator, I had an approval to make an assessment and selection between private conversations and conversations involving military personnel that were of no consequence for my command. That's the selection that I had the discretion to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you also make a selection in terms of the brief summaries that you made?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the second line of the third paragraph, you say: "I would just make a brief summary in a note-book if a conversation was not important." That's the second sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes. If I thought that the conversation was not important, I would just write a brief summary to summarise the contents if any of the things were mentioned in any of the subsequent conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that for a while you were without note-books. During the Srebrenica period, did you have note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: We didn't have note-books. We transcribed conversations on all sorts of things; on pieces of papers, in note-books, whatever we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also stated that there were tapes and that there were papers, and that note-books were archived in the command, and that the tapes were listened for important things?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The note-books that were filled up were archives -- archived, and the tapes were given to the command, and the command decided what should be left permanently recorded on the tapes. The rest was erased.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you personally destroy your notes or did you give your notes to the commanders to decide what to destroy if it was not important?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't think that the note-books were destroyed in my locations. They were forwarded to another location and they were archived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that the note-books were burned in your location?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't remember the note-books being burnt by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the 10th paragraph, the last two sentences: "I also recall a number of conversations relating to the fall of Srebrenica." And could you please tell us, when you say that people were infiltrating from the city, that the Serbs were infiltrated into that city, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: This is not about the infiltration into the city. This is about people who were fleeing Srebrenica, who joined the columns that were passing through. Some of them were VRS members that were infiltrated into those columns among those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. "There are also conversations regarding the placing of mines on routes those fleeing were expected to take, and requests made for buses to be provided." Thank you, end of quote. Could you please tell us where those mines were placed and whether we can find that information in the transcripts that are before us?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The mines were placed at the places where the VRS assumed that those columns would pass through. However, we heard in subsequent conversations that the entire column was able to bypass those mines. And as for the buses, I believe that there are conversations relative to the buses which were requested for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether these conversations are relative to those who attempted to leave Potocari and go in the direction of Tuzla or whether this concerns the others, those who tried to break through with the military column towards Tuzla. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't know who this concerned, whether they were trying to break through and go in from Potocari. In any case, they were trying to reach free territory. These were the columns discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you wrote the transcripts and you included this in the statement, it would be important for us to know who this pertains to. Is it the people who were evacuated aboard -- on board buses from Kladanj or those people trying to break through, who went via Crni Vrh and Baljkovica towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it had to do with those who were on foot. I don't think they would drive buses through minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So why did you mention the buses, then?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The buses were used to deport those who had been caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To where?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did all those buses go to Srebrenica, since you say that you knew well the voice of the person requesting that the buses be provided? Did he send buses to Srebrenica for all those who were at Crni Vrh and Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I know the person well by the voice, the person requesting those buses, and he probably needed them for certain parts around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did it have to do with the women, children, and the elderly who were taken on board -- aboard buses to Kladanj, or did it have to do with those soldiers who were on foot, trying to reach Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: It was for the women and children, but also able-bodied men were referred to, as well as certain figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you're saying this because of some assessments of yours or based on what you recorded and reflected in the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: This comes from the conversations I recorded and listened to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Out of these conversations, of which there are 11, can you indicate a passage which would have to do with that, to be able to see it for ourselves and see whether it concerns civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I didn't tell you precisely whom it concerned, but, yes, I can go back to the conversations and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me remind you. It is in that portion in which you speak of the Laser Company in Brcko and the 30 buses going towards Srebrenica. Perhaps you'll be able to find it now.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I need to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you find it, please read it out so as to avoid the need to put any further questions about it. We only have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I found it. The participants were X and Y: "Is there a possibility that we send some 10 buses?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: The other says: "Call them immediately. Apparently, there is 6.000 of them up to now." And the first one asked: "Are they able-bodied men?" The other says: "Keep quiet about this. Do not repeat."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: "All right, send them. I have three locations. It is where you and I were, and then the one at the crossroads, and then halfway to there. This is where they should be loaded, and at each of the locations there is between 1.000 and 1500 of them, and there are women and children being transported." And the other one says: "Yes, but there is more."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber which tab in your binder you were reading from. Which document was it? Perhaps it is tab number 7. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you to all who helped us. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were the buses sent to collect those from Potocari or to collect those you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't know who they were supposed to collect. They were requested, and I don't know who they transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the statement I quoted to you, you said that they transported -- well, see for yourself: "I don't know whether those buses were used, but I am familiar with some subsequent conversations in which it was confirmed that the buses took people to unknown destinations. I suppose it was also recorded." Can you tell us what those locations or destinations were?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely, because I don't have those conversations before me concerning that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I can tell you that we have witnesses from all those locations, and they speak of their manner -- means of transport. But since you intercepted this, are you sure that those who went on foot were then transferred onto buses?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't interested in how they moved about. I was interested in what we heard and recorded. Whether they transported able-bodied men, civilians, or women, later on in some other conversations it turned out that the buses were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm running out of time. Can you tell us which conversation it is, with what number, and then we'll check it ourselves, and the Chamber can do the same, so as not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which tab in your binder in front of you, the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in the radio network you used concerning Srebrenica, well, were you familiar with that and with its participants? Did you have that on one of your working maps?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Well, we had most of them, 90 per cent of the participants' code-names and frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have at least the main commanders of units engaged around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As part of the network, did you also have my position and my radio station frequency?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was it; can you tell the Chamber? Was it marked on your working map?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Apologies. Do you mean the frequency of the network or the name, the code-name?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Either way.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it was Panorama.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was Panorama a combat unit, or was it a command post, a location, a facility?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it was a command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it an office or working area or a unit in the field?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know. What do you mean, "a working place"? It was a command and the people who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When intercepting conversations from there, were you able to establish whether it was the main staff or an operational unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So what was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think it was an army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Among the conversations you intercepted, were there any conversations where I was a participant?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did it have to do with any combat operations or with some other activities concerning UNPROFOR and other sides to the conflict, in terms of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't study this in detail. But you are right, there are certain conversations concerning UNPROFOR and private conversations. There's lots of it, but I didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a conversation which would have to do with the engagement of units in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I apologise, but first I would have to refer to the conversations, themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There is no need. The four conversations that were admitted here -- first, seven were admitted, and then another four which were used only in this case and not the Popovic case, can you see those and do you know what they refer to?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I see one of those now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are tabs 8, 9, 10, 11 in the binder. Thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether they refer to combat or non-combat activities?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Sir, I looked at two out of four, and so far I didn't notice any combat activities. But these were regular activities in times of war. Anything happening in a war has to do with combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, what about humanitarian assistance; is that a combat activity?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the conditions in which it is forwarded. If it is in grave condition, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the two intercepts you just saw, did you notice any direct participation on my part or were there only go-betweens mentioning my name? Am I one of the participants or are the participants only referring to me?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: In the first few I saw, you are one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you say that I only spoke about the activities which did not have to do with the front-line and Srebrenica. Am I discussing any activities having to do with the front-lines and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: I apologise. I would have to refer to them first. I don't know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, the first two you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: In the first conversation, it was a private matter you discussed with this gentleman. He was asking something for you to do about his relative. As for the other one --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, following this answer I will have no further questions. By your leave, I would kindly ask that we wait for his reply. In case we're running too late, we can go without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Well, we are waiting for the reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I need some time to read all this and to see whether anything of that -- any of that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further interest in that. I would like to thank you for testifying here. I wish you a safe journey, and God bless. As far as I'm concerned, this closes my examination. I would like to thank the interpreters, on behalf of Defence, in trying to catch up with me and the witness. I would also like to thank all those who followed this testimony in these difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir, for your nice words. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: May I have just less than two minutes, Mr. President, to clear up one point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters and all the others, the court recorder, are fine with it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, there was one reference in the English transcript. It was page 82, and questions and answers at line 5 to 8. You were asked: "You say that you joined the unit in 1995, and ... for how long did you work without interruptions?" And you answered: "I believe that I worked up to sometime around the 8th or 9th June." Could you clarify whether this answer is correctly interpreted?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: It is not correct. I think it was July, rather than June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did your shift-work continue throughout July, during the period of the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PW-038
utterances.text: For as long as there was any activity and lots of work, this is how we worked. On some days, the intensity was lower, requiring less personnel because they were sufficient to have it all under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions. And with thanks to the Court's indulgence and to all the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you will be pleased that this concludes the questioning for you. You are now free to return to your home and to your normal activities. And, again, thank you for your attendance here. But please wait a moment before you leave the courtroom. As all others, I would like to thank all who assisted us in the quite difficult circumstances of today's hearing. It was, nevertheless, a very effective hearing. And especially I would like to say my gratitude to the interpreters and the court recorder. It was hard work today. And I have to inform everybody that I got information about the previous witness. We will not get any information about his possibility, if he is able to testify tomorrow. He is now in the hospital. And in these circumstances, we can't resume tomorrow. I take it, Mr. Tolimir, with really high gratitude, that you have contributed to the situation and that you indicated to agree that the witness should be free to return if his health permits his return to his home. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is still my position. Both the previous witness and this one can go home. It would really not be humane for us to keep him waiting until Tuesday or recall him from the hospital. There is really no urgency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Tolimir. The Chamber appreciates this position very much. We are finished today's hearing. Thank you all, and we wish you a good weekend. But we will resume next Tuesday, I think, at 9.00 in Courtroom I. We adjourn.
